item.title: I stopped losing articles I'd already read by building one searchable library
item.itunes:title: I stopped losing articles I'd already read by building one searchable library
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My work requires me to read a lot. Between researching articles, checking product announcements, reading technical documentation, and going down the occasional interesting rabbit hole, I come across more useful information than I can remember. For a while, I thought saving everything was enough. It wasn't. The real value of something I read often shows up weeks or months later, when I need that information for a completely different article. That's when I realized I needed a better way to keep my reading useful over time. I started using Zotero to build a personal research library, and it has changed how I handle the things I read.

My reading collection was scattered everywhere

I had information, not organization

For a long time, I treated everything I read as something I might need later, but I never had a consistent way to keep track of it. Interesting articles would stay open in browser tabs until I eventually closed them. PDFs would pile up in my Downloads folder, while screenshots, copied passages, and useful links ended up mixed in with unrelated files.

The problem became more noticeable when I started researching a topic I had covered before. I would vaguely remember reading something useful, but the details were gone. I knew it existed somewhere on my computer or online, yet finding it again often took longer than I expected.

I also had a habit of saving things with whatever filename or location was convenient at the time. That worked when I had only a handful of files. As the collection grew, though, those small decisions started making everything harder to manage. I wasn't losing information. I was losing track of where I'd put it.

Zotero became my library

My reading finally found a home

I eventually started using Zotero as the central place for the things I wanted to keep. I liked that it was built around references rather than simply acting like another folder on my computer. That made it feel much more suitable for the kind of material I collect while researching.

I began adding articles, research papers, reports, and other useful sources to my Zotero library. The browser connector made saving something I was reading fairly quick, so I didn't have to interrupt my reading just to organize it properly. For PDFs, I could keep the document alongside its related reference instead of treating the file as a standalone download.

Zotero keeps the information around a source together. Instead of having a document in one place and its details somewhere else, I could keep the source and its associated information connected. It gradually became my default destination for anything I considered worth keeping. I didn't need to rethink my entire setup. I simply changed where I saved useful reading material.

This open-source tool was built for academics, and it's the best productivity tool I own

I turned an academic tool into my everyday information keeper.

By  Yash Patel

Search replaced my folders

Finding things finally became effortless

The biggest change for me was how I started finding things. I no longer needed to remember which folder I had created, what I had named a file, or where I had decided to put it. I could simply search for the subject I remembered and let Zotero narrow things down.

If I wanted to find something I had saved about local AI models, I could search using a related keyword instead of trying to remember the exact title. The same worked when I only remembered an author, publication, or part of a title.

I still use collections to keep broad areas separated, but I don't spend much time building a complicated folder structure. I also use tags when I want to connect things that belong to different topics.

This has made my library much easier to navigate. Instead of organizing everything around where a file lives, I organize it around what the information is about. Search does most of the work now.

It fits my workflow

Works without changing my routine

Zotero works well for me because it doesn't force me to change how I research. As a tech blogger, I'm constantly jumping between product documentation, company announcements, research papers, technical articles, and reports. I can add useful material as I come across it without turning every reading session into an organizational task.

It also fits naturally into my writing process. When I start an article, I already have a place for relevant material while I'm researching. I can keep sources I may need later without creating a separate system for every project.

Another thing I like is that Zotero doesn't make me choose between reading and organizing. I can quickly save something and keep going with what I was doing. When I have more time, I can clean things up or add more context. That makes the whole setup feel practical rather than complicated.

4 Zotero plugins that are my productivity secret weapon

Zotero, but better

1
By  Yash Patel

I stopped losing good reads

I didn't need another complicated productivity system. I needed a simple way to make the information I come across useful beyond the moment I read it. Zotero gave me that without adding much friction to my day. Now, my reading feels more intentional, and I waste less time retracing my steps. For a blogger who is constantly researching, that small change has made a surprisingly big difference.

Zotero

Zotero collects sources and other metadata from research papers, webpages, etc., that can be inserted into documents in the form of citations.

item.title: I called the Steam Machine overpriced in July, and now it's the cheapest PC I'd actually buy
item.itunes:title: I called the Steam Machine overpriced in July, and now it's the cheapest PC I'd actually buy
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Nearly eighty days ago, the Steam Machine entered the market with a price of $1,049 and to most hardware reviewers and consumers at large, it seemed like the biggest joke of the decade. Most of Valve's marketing suggested that it was an absurd hybrid between a PC that had limited modularity, and a console that had no exclusive titles. Needless to say, no serious buyer was looking at it.

Eighty days later, the market has moved. The DRAM crisis has continued to take its toll, making a jump to the latest memory standard nearly impossible for millions of gamers. NAND flash prices have more or less continued to make storage upgrades difficult, and this year, nothing new has landed at the bottom of the GPU stack to reset expectations.

What has remained stagnant during this time, is the price of the Steam Machine, and that alone has warranted a second look at the GabeCube.

Steam Machine's price hasn't moved since its release

Meanwhile, everything around it got more expensive

Credit: Steam Store | Valve

Valve has been selling the Steam Machine for $1,049 since orders opened at the end of June, and that is a number that hasn't moved despite the components inside the box becoming considerably more expensive over the course of the last three months.

In the meantime, DDR5 and NAND prices have both been steadily climbing. TrendForce's third-quarter forecast has conventional DRAM contract prices up by 13–18% quarter-on-quarter and NAND flash up by 10-15%. On the other hand, things haven't gotten any better in the retail market either.

According to the latest price trend report from Tom's Hardware, DDR5 memory prices have risen sharply over the last trimester, with retailers raising prices to align with the current market conditions as consumers pay thrice or four times as much for the same standard and capacity.

Oddly enough, this has made the Steam Machine an interesting proposition as a prebuilt. It's worth a second look now for the same reason as you'd want a second look at any other mini PC, which is a locked price in a moving market. Since Valve locked the price before the memory and storage market decided to make everyone's lives difficult, consumers in the market for the Steam Machine right now are exempt from the subsequent rises in component prices since June.

So why not just simply look at a mini PC instead of a Steam Machine? Well, the answer to that is something that has changed for the GabeCube, and that's something that most mini PCs won't offer.

Someone built their own Steam Machine at Valve's original price point, and it's a solid contender

It has a fun name, too.

3
By  Simon Batt

FSR 4.1 changed the GabeCube's value equation

Most reviews tested it before the upscaler even arrived

  • Credit: Steam Store | Valve
  • Credit: Valve
  • Credit: Steam Store | Valve
  • Credit: Future
  • Credit: Steam Store | Valve
  • Credit: Valve
  • Credit: Steam Store | Valve
  • Credit: Future

The GPU is undoubtedly a primary consideration for any user who's looking to buy a dedicated gaming device, and that's another aspect where the Steam Machine seems to have evolved in terms of pure value proposition. When the device first came out, most reviewers tested it before the FSR 4.1 upscaler reached it.

AMD has since enabled its INT8 FSR 4.1 path on RDNA 3 in late June, and support for the Steam Machine has been confirmed through Proton Experimental. For those with a 4K TV, that's one aspect that can genuinely elevate the gameplay experience.

Perhaps the most crucial aspect of it all is paying attention to what FSR 4.1 costs to reach anywhere else. The upscaler currently runs on only two families of cards, including the Radeon RX 9000 series, which has had it since March, and the Radeon RX 7000 series, which received it in June. At today's retail prices, you're expecting to pay anywhere between $329 (for an entry-level RX 7000 series card) up to $779 for the RX 9000 series flagship.

I pushed FSR 4.1 and DLSS 4.5 to their limits on older hardware, and one changed my mind about 4K gaming

It was neck-and-neck, until it wasn't

6
By  Samarveer Singh

Storage expansion is an escape hatch from NAND inflation

A microSD card might be the cheapest way to add storage right now

On the storage side of things, Valve's desktop seems to be aging in the most consumer-friendly manner as well, in that, it doesn't force you to buy all your storage on day one.

The 512GB model works as a decent starting point, with one user-accessible NVMe slot left empty until NAND pricing returns to the affordable territory. Until then, the Machine offers a way to add storage capacity via microSDXC cards, and as of the time of writing, a $175 card can bump up your capacity by 1TB.

This means that, by owning a GabeCube, you defer the expensive upgrade, can comfortably expand your on-device game library, and fit a proper NVMe SSD whenever the market allows for it. Meanwhile, if you were to purchase an Xbox Series X or a PlayStation 5, you would be stuck with a fixed-storage console, with your only expansion options being limited to proprietary expansion cards or SSDs at vastly inflated prices.

SSD prices are still climbing, yet you are killing your drive for no good reason

Losing your existing SSD won't be pretty in this economy

1
By  Tanveer Singh

The cheapest gaming PC that you don't have to build

If you sat down to build a comparable system today, you'd need to sit with a spreadsheet, a browser full of price trackers, and enter the rabbit hold of waiting for a RAM kit or an NVMe drive to dip before the next contract hike changes the already uncertain PC hardware economy one more time.

This process itself has a cost, but right now, it seems that Valve is offering a subsidy on it. The Steam Machine at its current price delivers a current-gen upscaler, a cheap path to storage expansion, and a price that's 3 months old in a highly volatile component economy where prices change every other week. That's certainly a deal that I'd be sold on.

item.title: I had excellent Wi-Fi coverage everywhere and my Wi-Fi felt slow, but that coverage was part of the problem
item.itunes:title: I had excellent Wi-Fi coverage everywhere and my Wi-Fi felt slow, but that coverage was part of the problem
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My Wi-Fi setup looked perfect on paper. I had a strong signal in every room, barely any dead zones, and my phone almost always showed full bars. Yet something still fell off. Websites occasionally took longer to load, video calls weren’t as consistent as I expected, and speed tests varied far more than they should have.

Naturally, I assumed I needed better coverage. That turned out to be exactly the wrong approach.

Your mesh Wi-Fi's real problem is printed on the manufacturer's own website

Nobody prints it on the box.

By  Shivansh Raj Srivastava

I thought full bars meant my Wi-Fi was healthy

I kept adding coverage instead of questioning it

I mostly used the Wi-Fi signal icon as the easiest way to judge my network. If my phone showed full bars, I assumed everything was working properly. Whether I was in the bedroom, living room, kitchen, or even near the far end of the house, I usually had a strong signal.

That made the slowdowns even more confusing. Sometimes YouTube took a little longer to play a video. Downloads were not always as fast as I expected, and the connection could feel inconsistent when I moved from one room to another.

But because I had full bars, I never thought coverage could be part of the problem. In my mind, a strong signal automatically meant good Wi-Fi. So, I did what seemed logical at the time. I kept trying to improve the coverage even more. I added another mesh node and placed my access points so that every corner of the house had a strong signal.

I wanted to make sure there was almost no place where the Wi-Fi dropped below full strength. That was my mistake. I was focused on removing weak spots without thinking about what happened when several Wi-Fi points covered the same area.

My network looked better on my phone because the signal was strong everywhere, but behind the scenes, I had created too much overlap between my access points.

My access points were overlapping too much

More mesh nodes didn’t mean more bandwidth

Credit: 

Once I started looking deeper into my setup, I realized my access points were covering too much of the same area. I had placed them close enough that my phone could see several strong Wi-Fi signals at the same time. I thought that was a good thing because it meant there were no dead zones. In reality, it was making the network more crowded than it needed to be.

That is when I learned that a strong Wi-Fi signal doesn’t always mean fast Wi-Fi. The bars on my phone only showed how strong the connection was between my device and the access point. They did not tell me how busy that part of the network was, how much interference was present, or whether I was connected to the best access point in the house.

The roaming issue surprised me the most. My phone and laptop did not always jump to the nearest access point as soon as I moved to another room. Sometimes they stayed connected to the older one because its signal was still strong enough.

So, I could be standing close to one mesh node while my phone was still talking to another one farther away.

That explained why the network sometimes felt slow even with full bars. I had given my devices too many strong options, and they were not always choosing the best one. Once I stopped looking only at signal strength, the problem became much easier to understand.

I replaced my mesh Wi-Fi with a single high-end router, and the results surpassed my expectations

Performance improvements were well worth the switch.

12
By  Chandraveer Mathur

I moved my mesh nodes farther apart

I removed one node, and the network got better

When I dug more, I found that some of my nodes were sitting on the same or nearby channels, especially on the 2.4GHz band. That meant they were competing for the same airtime instead of working cleanly alongside each other.

On 2.4GHz, I made sure the access points were spread across non-overlapping channels. On 5GHz, I also tried to avoid having nearby nodes use the same channel where possible. I didn’t expect a huge difference, but the network immediately felt more consistent.

I had been running my access points at high power because I wanted the strongest possible signal everywhere. The problem was that every node was reaching much farther than it needed to. That created a lot of overlap. Dropping the transmit power helped shrink each Wi-Fi cell.

I also changed the physical placement of my mesh nodes. Instead of keeping them close together just to guarantee full bars, I moved them a little farther apart.

You can even go a step ahead and remove one mesh node completely. You may expect to see a dead zone somewhere, but that won’t be the case every time. The remaining nodes can already cover the house well enough. You can lose that unnecessary overlap and gain a cleaner network with less contention.

Perfect signal came with a catch

I used to think the goal of a good Wi-Fi setup was simple: get the strongest signal possible in every room. That turned out to be only half the story. The best part is that I didn’t have to sacrifice coverage to get better speeds. I still have a strong signal where I need it, but now the network feels faster, cleaner, and much more consistent.

item.title: KDE's LLM usage guidelines proposer asks people not to "burn each other to the ground" over discussing the new technology
item.itunes:title: KDE's LLM usage guidelines proposer asks people not to "burn each other to the ground" over discussing the new technology
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • KDE's draft LLM guidelines were locked a few days ago after things got a little heated.
  • Non-contributors inflamed the debate, leading to bans and a petition mostly signed by outsiders.
  • KDE must adapt to LLMs, with its guidelines proposer asking people not to fight in discussions.

LLM usage in open-source projects is a heated topic right now. Both sides have their points, and both sides are just as eager to debate them on internet forums. Recently, KDE made news after a thread proposing LLM guidelines was locked after quite a bit of drama. Now, the person behind the guidelines has made a new post explaining what happened and how things should go moving forward

Please don't fight each other during AI usage discussions, says Nate Graham

KDE is trying its best to navigate a new world of tech

In a Planet KDE post, developer Nate Graham explained what's happening with the discussion about KDE's LLM. A few days ago, Graham posted a first draft of LLM usage guidelines for feedback. While the discussion started perfectly civil, it got a little heated toward the end.

At the time, we called it a "fiery community clash," but Graham explains it was more nuanced. The discussion began among known KDE developers; it was civil and controlled. However, two people "unknown to any KDE contributors" began to bring up the ethics of LLM usage, and one "exposed the other person’s odious Twitter posts", causing both to be banned. To sum it up, Graham said that "A bunch of people mostly outside of KDE who disapprove of LLM usage derailed KDE’s attempt to add restrictions to LLM usage."

Graham also points to KDE for People, the sub-community set up to pressure KDE into dropping LLM usage. Graham notes that while the petition garnered a decent number of signatures, "almost none of whom are known KDE contributors," with Graham only recognising one of the signers.

Graham then notes that, while he understands that LLMs are not perfect and that he himself is concerned about the effect of AI as a whole, navigating a world with this new technology is like if "100 billion toaster-sized nuclear reactors dropped from the sky one day," and that KDE has no choice but to adapt. To round things off, Graham asks the following:

Please don’t derail the process.

Please don’t take it as an opportunity to fight over the broader topic of AI in general.

Please don’t try to burn each other to the ground over it.

Please don’t actually doxx or send hate mail to anyone over it, or try to get them fired from their job.

Please, just be kind.

With Graham's post, we now have a clearer picture of where this schism is happening. Instead of being between KDE's developers, it seems to be more between the people making KDE and its users who disapprove of AI usage. Navigating this gap is going to be tricky, and it'll be interesting to see whether KDE bends to anti-AI users' demands or places its developers' opinions first. As of right now, it seems to be taking the latter route.

GCC, the core compiler behind Linux, draws a hard line against AI code

No AI code here, thanks.

item.title: This open-source Microsoft 365 alternative is better than others because it stays boring
item.itunes:title: This open-source Microsoft 365 alternative is better than others because it stays boring
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve used enough office software to notice a pattern: every few years, the definition of a “modern” office suite gets bigger. What starts as a tool for documents and spreadsheets gradually picks up collaboration features, connected services, AI tools, and plenty of extras. That isn’t necessarily bad, but it isn’t always what I want. As someone who spends a lot of time writing, I’d rather have software that stays focused on the job instead of constantly trying to expand its role.

That’s what caught my attention with LibreOffice. It feels almost stubbornly traditional in a market where software is expected to keep evolving into something bigger. And surprisingly, that’s exactly what I like about it. LibreOffice doesn’t need to be exciting to be useful, and its boring nature is becoming one of its biggest advantages.

LibreOffice refuses to become cloud software

Not everything needs to be online

One thing I appreciate about LibreOffice is that it hasn't tried to follow the same path as most modern office suites. It doesn't feel like it's constantly pushing me toward a web version or trying to turn the desktop app into a gateway for an online service. When I use Writer or Calc, the focus stays on the actual application and the work I'm doing.

I find that refreshing because I don't need my office suite to keep adding layers around basic document editing. I don't need a built-in workspace, online dashboard, or a collection of connected services just to write an article or work on a spreadsheet.

LibreOffice feels comfortable staying in a traditional desktop office suite. That might sound unexciting compared with newer productivity software, but I actually prefer it. It does its job without constantly trying to reinvent what an office suite is supposed to be.

It proves that offline isn't a limitation

Local software gives me more control

I’ve realized that being offline doesn’t have to mean being unable to get work done. A lot of my writing happens at my desk, and I don’t need an internet connection just to draft an article, edit a document, or work through a spreadsheet. LibreOffice lets me keep working exactly as I normally would.

I also find this useful when I’m traveling or dealing with an unreliable connection. I can open my files and continue working instead of waiting for a service to load or worrying about whether everything is available at that moment.

This approach also offers a privacy benefit. My documents can stay within my own setup instead of automatically becoming part of an online service. That gives me more control over drafts, research notes, and other files I’m working with. LibreOffice is also an open-source office suite. For me, that combination of offline access, local control, and open-source development makes it feel like a more private way to work.

My docs don’t need an account for everything

Just open and work

Another thing I like about LibreOffice is how little personal information it asks from me. I can install it, open Writer, and start working without creating an account first. That sounds like a small detail, but it makes the whole experience feel much simpler.

I’ve become used to software asking me to sign in before I can access basic features. Sometimes I just want to create a document without connecting it to another account or setting up another profile. LibreOffice doesn’t make that part of the process complicated.

It doesn’t try to be another productivity ecosystem

Office suite can just be office

LibreOffice doesn’t try to become the center of everything I do. I already have separate tools for notes, task management, file storage, communication, and other parts of my workflow. I don’t need my office suite to replace all of them.

When I’m writing in Writer, I want a good writing environment. When I’m working in Calc, I want a capable spreadsheet tool. That’s pretty much it. LibreOffice doesn’t constantly push me to add more services or change how I organize the rest of my work.

That makes it easier to fit LibreOffice into my existing setup. I can use it alongside the tools I already prefer instead of rebuilding my workflow around one platform. For me, that focus is a strength. LibreOffice doesn’t need to become an all-in-one productivity system to remain useful.

item.title: Google’s new experimental Gemini Intelligence feature makes the phone calls you’d rather avoid
item.itunes:title: Google’s new experimental Gemini Intelligence feature makes the phone calls you’d rather avoid
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Gemini's "Call for Me" handles the entire call, including menus, hold time, and conversation.
  • The feature feels dystopian and requires a lot of trust, but it shows live transcripts and lets you take over at any time.
  • An early preview of Call for Me on the Pixel 11 in the U.S. for Gemini paid subscribers in Phone by Google beta; wider release unclear.

I dislike talking on the phone, but what I really hate is getting stuck on hold when I have a simple, menial task to take care of, like rescheduling a doctor's appointment or booking servicing for my car. With that in mind, Direct My Call could be the AI-powered Gemini Intelligence feature I've been waiting for — though at the same time, it's also pretty weird.The experimental new feature, Call for Me, builds on Hold for Me and Direct My Call by handling the entire call for you, including menu navigation and speaking on your behalf. It's a bit dystopian and requires a tremendous amount of trust from both the user and the person on the other end of the call, but I can also see it being genuinely useful for simple tasks.

Google offers up examples like checking a hardware store's stock of a specific part, reserving a seat at a restaurant, or shifting a haircut appointment to another day. According to the tech giant, Gemini makes the call for you, introduces itself, navigates automated phone menus, waits on hold, and even handles the entire conversation with the person at the other end.

Google says trust and control are key to Call for Me

It still feels rather dystopian, though

Google emphasizes that "you remain in control at all times" and says that a live transcript view is available, too. You can also take over the conversation at any point, though I can see that leading to a rather awkward situation. It's also worth pointing out that the person on the other end taking this kind of service-oriented call, whether it's rescheduling an appointment at the bank or booking a patio table at a restaurant, likely won't have much patience for a robot that's not communicating effectively. It seems like this is something Google has considered, though.

"Just as importantly, every phone call connects two sides. For this to work, it has to respect the time of the neighborhood shops and front-desk staff answering the phone. These calls made by Gemini on behalf of the user represent real customers conducting real transactions: booking appointments, placing items on hold, or rescheduling reservations," writes Google in a press release.Call for Me is rolling out in early preview to Gemini paid subscribers who are enrolled in the Phone by Google Public Beta program on the Pixel 11 series in the US. It's unclear when the feature will be released more widely.

item.title: My RTX 4070 Ti was heading for retirement until I unlocked Nvidia's restricted frame generation
item.itunes:title: My RTX 4070 Ti was heading for retirement until I unlocked Nvidia's restricted frame generation
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I built my RTX 4070 Ti-powered GPU back in 2023, you could have mailed me at P.O. Box Cloud 9. I'd just bought one of the best GPUs on the market, and it could generate frames when I needed it to. Last week, however, I stopped using the word "beefy" for it. My RTX 4070 Ti is hardly ancient, but The Blood of Dawnwalker was the first game that made me feel like I was genuinely running into its limits.

At 4K, even DLSS 4.5 wasn't enough to give me the sort of performance I wanted, and conventional frame generation only took me so far. Naturally, I started messing with things Nvidia never intended my card to have. What happened next was ridiculous enough to make me question whether we're being too quick to write off older GPUs. Thanks to the right mods and OptiScaler, I pushed Multi Frame Generation far beyond what the RTX 4070 Ti officially supports, and the results had me back at my old address in the clouds.

I ran DLSS 5 on my PS2 games, and they finally looked like I remembered them

Nostalgia, meet neural rendering

11
By  Samarveer Singh

My RTX 4070 Ti was starting to buckle at 4K

The latest Unreal Engine 5 title exposed where my GPU was running out of road

It had been a while since I contended with a fresh new Unreal Engine 5 title, and The Blood of Dawnwalker is exactly the kind of game I'd been looking forward to. Sadly, it also makes my perfectly respectable GPU suddenly feel considerably less respectable. At 4K with DLAA, my RTX 4070 Ti averaged just about 40 FPS. It's not completely unplayable, but it's nowhere near where I want a demanding modern game to sit on a card that I intend to use for another two full years.

Using DLSS 4.5 at its Quality Preset is what pushed me past the 60 FPS mark, but the 1% lows were still comfortably dipping into 40 FPS territory. Then, I threw my final tool at the wall, and regular DLSS Frame Generation at 2x gave me around 90 FPS, with my 1% lows being consistently above 60 FPS as well.

The problem, however, remained combat, where the frame rate would dip and stutter. The usual Unreal Engine 5 quirks aside, the game itself felt tough to stomach without Frame Generation, and even then, the base frame rate of around 65 FPS left much to be desired.

DLSS 4.5 really helped me move on from 1440p to permanently gaming at 4K, but at 2160p, Dawnwalker was asking if I could make the big numbers on the frame counter feel useful. I just had no idea that my answer would involve 4x Multi Frame Generation.

I pushed FSR 4.1 and DLSS 4.5 to their limits on older hardware, and one changed my mind about 4K gaming

It was neck-and-neck, until it wasn't

6
By  Samarveer Singh

I somehow got 4x MFG running on my RTX 4070 Ti

The results were far more convincing than Nvidia would have me believe

The fun only started when I consciously stopped treating the RTX 4070 Ti like Nvidia's software wanted me to. I used OptiScaler to get Multi Frame Generation working, alongside the DLSS Libraries and RenoDX to throw in the DLSS 5 Neural Rendering DLL file for good measure. Just like that, my "unsupported" 40-series GPU was doing something it absolutely shouldn't.

At 4K, I could now go all the way up to 3x Frame Generation instead of just 2x, which is exactly what I pushed my GPU to. My average performance jumped to almost 140 FPS, while the base frame rate remained at around 44 FPS. The trade-off, of course, was the latency, which climbed to over 30 ms. As was evident, the bigger the generated-frame multiplier, the less representative the headline FPS number becomes.

To me, 3x Frame Generation felt like the perfect sweet spot, especially considering 4x MFG pushed my GPU just 100 MB shy of running into its VRAM limit. With 3x Frame Generation, the foliage held stable, the sharpness was exactly where I wanted it, and combat and traversal both felt just smooth enough for me to enjoy playing the game without fretting about VRAM usage or GPU power draw. The base render rate was only 40 FPS, but visually, the jump was absurd.

In trying to make 4K more usable for my PC and on my 3-year-old GPU, Multi Frame Generation finally became more than just an unachievable distant feature, and ended up giving me a ton of extra runway.

Nvidia's 6x frame generation proves that we've reached the hardware ceiling for GPUs

There's only so much VRAM to go around.

39
By  Samarveer Singh

My RTX 4070 Ti just got the second wind I was hoping for

I can coast until the RTX 60 series now

Successfully using Multi Frame Generation on an RTX 40 series GPU is nothing if not a second wind. My RTX 4070 Ti clearly has enough hardware to make 3x and 4x MFG useful, and the fact that I can push it even further with 6x makes the card feel considerably less obsolete. I know it won't behave exactly like an RTX 50-series GPU running native MFG, but I don't need it to, either. I needed it to get Dawnwalker running properly at 4K, and it does exactly that.

That changes how I see this card's remaining lifespan. I bought an RTX 4070 Ti to last several years at 1440p, but I'll admit that the RTX 50-series became rather attractive just because Nvidia added another frame-generation multiplier. If an unofficial MFG mod can give me the extra headroom I need, I'm perfectly happy coasting along until the RTX 60 series gives me an actual hardware-backed reason to upgrade.

RTX 40-series cards can also run DLSS 5's "exclusive" Neural Rendering through OptiScaler, DLSS Swapper, or ReShade, depending on the game.

That said, I can't pretend Nvidia's approach doesn't annoy me. item.title: I ditched my old dashcam for one with a cable so thin it actually disappears
item.itunes:title: I ditched my old dashcam for one with a cable so thin it actually disappears
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Dashcams can be annoying to install, even on a good day. While installing the camera itself barely takes a few minutes, if you like clean cables, running thick USB cables through cladding, especially in older cars, is never fun.

That's why the new 70mai A900 Ultra immediately caught my attention. Instead of a conventional USB-style or even coaxial connection between the front and rear cameras, 70mai's latest opts for an LVDS digital transmission cable. A much thinner cable, 70mai further claims that this LVDS cable can transfer 4K footage with as low as 20ms of latency.

Look, this is the first time I've used an LVDS cable, so I was understandably skeptical of 70mai's claims. A week of use later, though, I can attest that the upgrade is no joke. Not only does the 70mai A900 Ultra's cable effectively disappear into the car's trim, but I'm also observing a clearer image with much lower lag when swapping between front and rear cameras.

The ultra-thin cable is a bigger upgrade than you'd think

Clean installation without compromising image quality

The biggest advantage of the 70mai A900 Ultra is also its most obvious one. And you don't need to install the camera to see it. Running a rear camera cable through a car is time-consuming, and every bend adds another spot where the cable can bunch up or not slot in easily.

The A900 Ultra's LVDS connection easily routes along the roofline. In fact, the cable is so thin that I could easily roll up extra cable and slide it into the roofliner out of sight. This wouldn't be possible with a conventional cable. But a thinner cable doesn't mean that you're making compromises. This cable is central to the A900 Ultra's high-speed digital transmission between the front and rear cameras. It's also critical to enabling that low 20ms latency for seamless switching.

The 70mai uses high-end Sony Starvis 2 IMX678 sensors for both the front and rear cameras, along with 4K HDR recording on both channels. So a fully digital interconnect becomes even more important to avoid quality loss. That makes sense since excessive low-light compression risks making the dashcam useless, as you wouldn't even be able to see license plates.

The rear camera has become indispensable

Low-latency footage makes it useful beyond simple recordings

My previous dashcam didn't include a rear camera, so this is new territory for me, and it's already made me consider how I went without one.

Where I live, I regularly deal with traffic that would make you want to give up driving, including motorcycles zigzagging through gaps and cars getting right up close and personal. A rear camera gives me another perspective when an incident happens. Obviously, a rear camera is useless in that scenario.

The lack of latency has another benefit. I've taken to toggling on the rear camera anytime I'm backing up, even though my car has a built-in reverse camera. The 70mai A900 Ultra's rear camera sensor is a massive upgrade over the one in my car and gives me much better ambient awareness when navigating tricky situations. Add to that the lack of latency, and it's a very good experience.

Of course, the dashcam does all standard dashcam things very well too. For example, with parking surveillance enabled, the system can monitor my car when I'm away. Elsewhere, the camera offers plenty of connectivity options. I particularly appreciate the 5GHz Wi-Fi 6 connection because it makes offloading footage extremely quick, instead of having to pull out the SD card every time.

The cable got me interested, but the package is what made it stick

Look, dashcams aren't something that you upgrade all that often. It's an appliance that sits around and passively records footage you'll hopefully never need. So, to convince me to upgrade my setup, it would need to be a significant upgrade. That's precisely what the 70mai A900 Ultra is.

While I was initially intrigued by the ease of installation via the LVDS cable, that's just one part of the equation. The high-speed, low-latency slim cable helps the rear camera maintain a high-bandwidth 4K connection to the front camera. This helps with recording and with using the rear camera for assistance when backing out of tight, tricky spots. Couple that with a high-end Starvis sensor, and you've got all the makings of an excellent and, more importantly, responsive dashcam setup.

These features are exactly what I've been looking for in a dashcam, and what makes the 70mai A900 Ultra such an excellent upgrade. All that said, I bought the dashcam for the ultra-slim cable, but the overall package is what makes it stick.

70mai A900 Ultra

The 70mai A900 Ultra is a dual channel dashcam with Sony Starvis 2 sensors and an LVDS cable interconnection between the rear camera and front module.

The cable got me interested, but the package is what made it stick

Look, dashcams aren't something that you upgrade all that often. It's an appliance that sits around and passively records footage you'll hopefully never need. So, to convince me to upgrade my setup, it would need to be a significant upgrade. That's precisely what the 70mai A900 Ultra is.

While I was initially intrigued by the ease of installation via the LVDS cable, that's just one part of the equation. The high-speed, low-latency slim cable helps the rear camera maintain a high-bandwidth 4K connection to the front camera. This helps with recording and with using the rear camera for assistance when backing out of tight, tricky spots. Couple that with a high-end Starvis sensor, and you've got all the makings of an excellent and, more importantly, responsive dashcam setup.

These features are exactly what I've been looking for in a dashcam, and what makes the 70mai A900 Ultra such an excellent upgrade. All that said, I bought the dashcam for the ultra-slim cable, but the overall package is what makes it stick.
